passages.happening:
God sends Moses to Pharaoh: “Let My people go, so that they may worship Me” (verse 1). If Pharaoh refuses, “the hand of the LORD will bring a severe plague on your livestock in the field” (verse 3). “But the LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt” (verse 4).

“The LORD set a time, saying, ‘Tomorrow the LORD will do this in the land’” (verse 5). “And the next day the LORD did just that. All the livestock of the Egyptians died, but not one animal belonging to the Israelites died” (verse 6).

Pharaoh sends officials to check and learns that none of Israel's animals died. “But Pharaoh’s heart was hardened, and he would not let the people go” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
The plagues are growing heavier. They now strike Egypt's wealth.

The list of animals in verse 3 is a list of riches, transport and power. Horses pulled the chariots that were a key part of Egypt's army in this period. The mention of camels is debated, because most evidence for camels kept by people in this region comes from later centuries, though camels were known earlier. Some think a later copyist updated the word. Others note that a few camels could have been there long before they were common.

Livestock were wealth, and some cattle were sacred. The Apis bull was worshiped at Memphis, and the goddess Hathor was often pictured as a cow. Many readers see this plague as a blow at those symbols too, though the text itself stresses Egypt's loss and Israel's escape rather than any one god.

God sets a time: ‘Tomorrow’. Again, nothing is left to chance. And again, a distinction: not one of Israel's animals dies. Pharaoh sends people to check. He knows. And still his heart was ‘hardened’. The Hebrew word is ‘heavy’ again.

A small puzzle: ‘All the livestock of the Egyptians died’, yet animals suffer again in the hail and the last plague. Many readers take ‘all’ as the sweeping way Hebrew stories often speak, or as meaning the animals ‘in the field’ named in verse 3.
passages.later:
Israel remembered: “He abandoned their cattle to the hail and their livestock to bolts of lightning” (Psalm 78:48), part of the psalm's long retelling of what God did in Egypt.

The distinction God made between Israel and Egypt points ahead to the night of the Passover (Exodus 12:13).
passages.asks: Pharaoh checked the facts and still would not change. Ask whether you have ever known the truth and refused to act on it. And ask what keeps a heart heavy even when the evidence is plain.

passages.t: Boils, and ‘the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart’
passages.happening:
God tells Moses and Aaron, “Take handfuls of soot from the furnace; in the sight of Pharaoh, Moses is to toss it into the air” (verse 8). It will become fine dust over Egypt, “and festering boils will break out on man and beast” (verse 9).

They do it, and the boils break out (verse 10). “The magicians could not stand before Moses, because the boils had broken out on them and on all the Egyptians” (verse 11).

“But the LORD hardened Pharaoh’s heart, and he would not listen to them, just as the LORD had said to Moses” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
This is the third plague of the second group, and like the others in that place it comes with no warning.

The soot comes from a furnace or kiln, the kind used for firing bricks or pots, and so perhaps from the very work built on Israel's forced labor. Deuteronomy later calls Egypt ‘the iron furnace’ (Deuteronomy 4:20). Moses throws the soot into the air in Pharaoh's sight. It is a sign acted out in public.

The magicians are back, but only to fall. They ‘could not stand before Moses’. The experts of Egypt are struck down by the plague themselves.

And then, for the first time in the plagues, the narrator says it plainly: ‘the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart’. God said in 4:21 that he would. Up to now the text has said that Pharaoh's heart was hard, or that Pharaoh hardened it himself. Only now, at the sixth plague, does it say that God did.
passages.later:
The boils became a byword for suffering. Deuteronomy warns, “The LORD will afflict you with the boils of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 28:27).

Paul writes of the hardening in Romans 9: “So then, it does not depend on man’s desire or effort, but on God’s mercy” (Romans 9:16), and “He hardens whom He wants to harden” (Romans 9:18).
passages.hard:
If God hardened Pharaoh's heart, how can Pharaoh be held responsible?

Exodus describes the hardening in three ways. God announces ahead of time that he will harden Pharaoh's heart (4:21; 7:3). The text says that Pharaoh's heart was hard or became hard, without naming a cause (7:13, 14, 22; 8:19; 9:7, 35). It says that Pharaoh hardened his own heart (8:15, 32; 9:34). And from this verse on, it says that the LORD hardened Pharaoh's heart (9:12; 10:1, 20, 27; 11:10; 14:4, 8). Through the first five plagues the narrator never says God did it. Pharaoh's own resistance comes first.

Christians weigh this in different ways. Many see a judicial hardening: God gives Pharaoh over to the road he has already chosen, strengthening a will that is truly Pharaoh's own, so that the hardening is itself a judgment. This is often the reading of those in the Arminian tradition, and of many Jewish readers. Others, especially in the Augustinian and Reformed traditions, stress Paul's use of this chapter in Romans 9, and hold that God's sovereign purpose stands behind Pharaoh's choices without making them any less Pharaoh's, so that he remains fully guilty. Some Jewish and Christian interpreters add a point from the verb meaning ‘make strong’: God kept Pharaoh from simply giving way out of fear, so that his decisions showed what was really in his heart, not panic.

Exodus itself does not settle the question with philosophy. It holds God's rule and Pharaoh's guilt together, and it never presents Pharaoh as a victim. Faithful Christians differ here, and these notes take no side.
passages.asks: The experts who copied God's signs could not stand at the end. Ask what you have been leaning on that will not stand when trouble comes. And if the hardening of Pharaoh's heart troubles you, ask what it would mean to keep your own heart soft toward God today.

passages.t: ‘There is no one like Me in all the earth’
passages.happening:
Moses meets Pharaoh early in the morning (verse 13). God's message is long this time: “Otherwise, I will send all My plagues against you and your officials and your people, so you may know that there is no one like Me in all the earth. For by this time I could have stretched out My hand and struck you and your people with a plague to wipe you off the earth. But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth” (verses 14-16).

“Still, you lord it over My people” (verse 17). Tomorrow God will send “the worst hail that has ever fallen on Egypt” (verse 18). “So give orders now to shelter your livestock and everything you have in the field” (verse 19).

“Those among Pharaoh’s officials who feared the word of the LORD hurried to bring their servants and livestock to shelter, but those who disregarded the word of the LORD left their servants and livestock in the field” (verses 20-21).
passages.hearers:
The third group of plagues begins, again with a morning meeting.

For the first time God explains why he has not simply wiped Egypt out. He could have done it already. He has held back for a purpose: that Pharaoh, and the whole earth, would come to know who he is. ‘I have raised you up’ is in Hebrew, I have made you stand. The magicians ‘could not stand’ (verse 11). Pharaoh stands only because God lets him.

Then something new: a warning that offers a way out. Bring your servants and animals in, and they will live. This is the first time Egyptians are given a way to escape a plague. And some take it. Among Pharaoh's own officials, some ‘feared the word of the LORD’. Others did not.

So the line between those who are spared and those who are not is no longer only the line between Israel and Egypt. It also runs through Egypt itself, between those who listen and those who do not. God's warning was given so that people could escape.
passages.later:
Paul quotes verse 16 in Romans: “For the Scripture says to Pharaoh: ‘I raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power in you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth’” (Romans 9:17).

God's purpose was that his name would be known everywhere. The New Testament sees that purpose reaching its goal in Jesus, whom God has given “the name above all names” (Philippians 2:9), “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow” (Philippians 2:10).
passages.asks: Before the hail, any Egyptian who feared God's word could find shelter. Ask whether you have heard a warning from God and treated it lightly. And ask what it means that God warns before he judges, so that people can escape.

passages.t: Hail and fire, and Goshen spared
passages.happening:
Moses stretches his staff toward heaven, “and the LORD sent thunder and hail, and lightning struck the earth” (verse 23). “The hail was so severe that nothing like it had ever been seen in all the land of Egypt from the time it became a nation” (verse 24).

The hail strikes down “everything in the field, both man and beast; it beat down every plant of the field and stripped every tree” (verse 25).

“The only place where it did not hail was in the land of Goshen, where the Israelites lived” (verse 26).
passages.hearers:
Hail is rare in Egypt, which is part of why this storm is so terrifying. Lightning flashes through it. The text stresses that nothing like it had been seen since Egypt became a nation. Egypt's history as one kingdom already stretched back more than a thousand years, so that is a strong claim.

This plague takes human lives as well as animals and crops. The text does not hide that. It also reminds us that people were warned, and that some listened.

And Goshen, once again, is spared. God makes a distinction. The storm stops at the edge of the land where his people live.
passages.later:
Israel's songs remember the storm: “He gave them hail for rain, with lightning throughout their land. He struck their vines and fig trees and shattered the trees of their country” (Psalm 105:32-33).

Revelation's last plagues echo this one: “great hailstones weighing almost a hundred pounds each rained down on them from above” (Revelation 16:21).
passages.asks: The storm stopped at the edge of Goshen. Ask what it would mean for you to trust God's care in a storm that is falling all around you. And ask how you can be a shelter for others while it lasts.

passages.happening:
“Then Pharaoh summoned Moses and Aaron. ‘This time I have sinned,’ he said. ‘The LORD is righteous, and I and my people are wicked. Pray to the LORD, for there has been enough of God’s thunder and hail. I will let you go’” (verses 27-28).

Moses says he will spread out his hands to the LORD, “so that you may know that the earth is the LORD’s. But as for you and your officials, I know that you still do not fear the LORD our God” (verses 29-30).

The flax and barley were destroyed, “since the barley was ripe and the flax was in bloom; but the wheat and spelt were not destroyed, because they are late crops” (verses 31-32).

Moses prays and the storm stops. “When Pharaoh saw that the rain and hail and thunder had ceased, he sinned again and hardened his heart” (verse 34).
passages.hearers:
Pharaoh's words sound like real repentance: ‘This time I have sinned’ and ‘The LORD is righteous’. But Moses sees through them: ‘you still do not fear the LORD’. Pharaoh is sorry about the hail. He is not sorry for what he has done to Israel. Verse 34 shows what his confession was worth.

‘Spread out my hands’ describes the common ancient way of praying: standing with open hands raised toward heaven.

‘The earth is the LORD's.’ Pharaoh thought Egypt was his. The storm has shown whose it is.

The little note about the crops is a window on the calendar. In Egypt barley ripens before wheat. So the hail fell in late winter or early spring, a few weeks before the Passover in the month of Abib. It also explains why the locusts of chapter 10 still find something to eat. Flax mattered because linen was Egypt's main cloth. Barley was used for bread and beer.

And once more the pressure lifts, and once more Pharaoh hardens his heart, he and his officials too.
passages.later:
The psalm says what Moses said to Pharaoh: “The earth is the LORD’s, and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1).

Paul describes the same posture of prayer: “I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands” (1 Timothy 2:8).

Paul also describes two kinds of sorrow: “Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death” (2 Corinthians 7:10).
passages.asks: Pharaoh said, ‘I have sinned’, and meant only that he wanted the hail to stop. Ask whether your own sorrow for sin is sorrow for what you did, or only for what it cost you. And ask what real repentance would look like in one area of your life this week.
